label: pathplanning
summary: A Python motion-planning toolkit: describe a world, choose a planner, validate a route, and learn from the result.

children.label: The agent loop
children.summary: An autonomous agent observes a world, builds a planning problem, chooses a route, checks it, moves, then observes again.

children.label: Observe
children.summary: Read the map or state the agent currently knows. The world model may become stale after the robot moves.

children.label: Model the problem
children.summary: Choose states, legal actions, motion rules, costs, and goal conditions. These choices define what a planner can know.

children.label: Plan
children.summary: Select a supported algorithm that fits the graph, robot, timing rules, and number of agents.

children.label: Validate
children.summary: Check endpoints, legal motions, collisions, timing, and objective cost with the problem's independent rules.

children.label: Act
children.summary: Execute a safe part of the route. The planner returns a path; a controller decides how to follow it.

children.label: Observe again
children.summary: If the world or goal changes, decide whether the old plan is still valid or a new planning call is needed.

children.label: Worlds & problem models
children.summary: Algorithms operate on a model of states and legal moves, not on a picture of the real world.

children.label: Discrete graphs
children.summary: A graph exposes nodes, neighbors, and edge costs. Grid worlds are one useful graph representation.

children.label: Grid2DSearchSpace
children.summary: A reference graph for 2D cell movement, corner rules, and optional terrain costs.

children.label: 3D grids
children.summary: Voxel worlds expose 3D cell neighbors and their movement costs.

children.label: Costs & heuristics
children.summary: Edge costs say what a move costs; a heuristic estimates remaining cost and has algorithm-specific correctness rules.

children.label: Continuous spaces
children.summary: A space can sample free states, check motions, measure distance, and steer between states.

children.label: 2D, 3D, and N-D
children.summary: Spaces represent configurations in two dimensions, three dimensions, or a general state vector.

children.label: Obstacles & motion checks
children.summary: A state may be valid while the motion between two valid states still collides with an obstacle.

children.label: Goal regions
children.summary: A goal can be an exact state or a region that contains many acceptable states.

children.label: Vehicles & motion primitives
children.summary: Some robots can only move through trajectories allowed by their steering, speed, and acceleration limits.

children.label: Ackermann / SE(2)
children.summary: Vehicle states include position and heading; motions must respect steering and body-size constraints.

children.label: State lattice
children.summary: A finite set of sampled local-frame motion primitives defines the allowed local moves.

children.label: Dynamics & time
children.summary: Velocity and acceleration affect which motions can be followed and where the robot may safely wait.

children.label: Time & safe intervals
children.summary: A location can be safe at one time and blocked at another. Timed edges have durations; blocked intervals define when movement is unsafe.

children.label: Several agents
children.summary: Plans must account for the team moving together, including vertex conflicts and edge-swap conflicts.

children.label: Planner atlas
children.summary: The registry is the supported planner surface. Use the atlas to compare each planner's idea, limits, and project-specific contract.

children.label: Public API & contracts
children.summary: Typed problem contracts, registry dispatch, planner parameters, result objects, and optional trace callbacks form the public boundary.

children.label: Planning entry points
children.summary: Public calls validate a problem and dispatch to its registered planner.

children.label: Planner registry
children.summary: The registry declares supported IDs, problem kinds, and callable adapters.

children.label: Problem contracts
children.summary: DiscreteProblem and ContinuousProblem describe the world, start, goal, and optional settings.

children.label: Parameters & results
children.summary: Planner settings and PlanResult keep behavior, stop reasons, metrics, and paths explicit.

children.label: Trace callbacks
children.summary: Opt-in trace events expose selected planning progress without loading visualization at import time.

children.label: Python and native engines
children.summary: Python owns the API contracts and adapters. Native engines own the hot search and sampling loops behind a documented ABI.

children.label: Python validation & adapters
children.summary: Validate inputs, prepare native models, adapt results, and keep custom callback use explicit.

children.label: C ABI / FFI
children.summary: Private ctypes declarations connect Python data layouts to native functions.

children.label: C++ graph search
children.summary: Native discrete graph and kinodynamic search engines own frontiers, search state, and CSR data.

children.label: C sampling engine
children.summary: Native sampling kernels own planner expansion, tree storage, edge queues, and built-in collision work.

children.label: ABI, ownership & errors
children.summary: Versioning and ownership rules keep native layouts and Python declarations aligned.

children.label: Metrics & replay traces
children.summary: Native metrics and trace interfaces expose measured work and selected search events.

children.label: Geometry & data structures
children.summary: Reusable geometric curves, nearest-neighbor indexes, queues, and tree storage support multiple planner families.

children.label: Curves & vehicle paths
children.summary: Bezier, B-spline, cubic, polynomial, Dubins, and Reeds-Shepp path tools.

children.label: Nearest-neighbor indexes
children.summary: Sampling planners use reusable nearest-neighbor support for large sets of states.

children.label: Queues & priority queues
children.summary: FIFO, LIFO, and priority queues organize frontier work for search algorithms.

children.label: Tree storage
children.summary: Array-backed tree structures keep large sampled search trees compact.

children.label: Datasets & evaluation
children.summary: The project records separate benchmark cohorts and checks routes against problem-specific correctness oracles.

children.label: Dataset inventory
children.summary: MovingAI, BARN, Monash, OMPL, and DIMACS collections have different world models and data lineage.

children.label: Frozen protocols
children.summary: Inputs, versions, hashes, seeds, and workload selection are recorded before runs.

children.label: Independent route checks
children.summary: Validate endpoints, collisions, legal transitions, timing, and reconstructed cost with an independent check.

children.label: What gets measured
children.summary: Keep solved coverage beside latency, path quality, work counters, memory, timeouts, and missing results.

children.label: Keep cohorts separate
children.summary: Grid, road-graph, voxel, temporal, and continuous workloads use different costs and correctness rules; they are not one leaderboard.

children.label: Visualization, examples & tests
children.summary: Learn by watching a route, try the API in examples, and use focused tests to check contracts and regressions.

children.label: Render, replay, inspect
children.summary: Visualization stays optional and is loaded through explicit rendering or replay calls.

children.label: Runnable examples
children.summary: Small examples show custom worlds, planner calls, and rendered routes.

children.label: Contract & regression tests
children.summary: Focused tests cover public contracts, search behavior, native ABI, benchmarks, and visualization.

children.label: Project guides
children.summary: Architecture, planner support, native boundaries, and benchmark rules live in versioned documentation.
